topics.title: Why RAG?
topics.concept: Retrieval-Augmented Generation connects an LLM to external evidence at inference time. An ingestion pipeline parses, chunks, embeds and indexes documents. At query time the system retrieves relevant evidence and supplies it to the model. This addresses private or frequently changing knowledge and improves traceability, but does not guarantee correctness.
topics.example: An employee asks “How many carry-forward leave days are allowed?” Instead of guessing from training data, the assistant searches the latest HR policy and cites the specific clause.
topics.interviewAnswer: I use RAG when answers depend on proprietary or frequently updated information. I index source documents, retrieve relevant passages for each query, and instruct the LLM to answer from those passages with citations. Unlike fine-tuning, RAG updates knowledge without retraining. I evaluate retrieval recall and answer faithfulness separately, and abstain when evidence is insufficient.
steps: Ingest and normalize trusted documents; preserve source/version metadata
Split documents into meaningful units and embed/index them
Retrieve, filter and rerank passages for each user query
Generate a grounded answer with source references and abstention logic
tradeoffs: RAG is not a substitute for fine-tuning behavior or output style
Retrieval can miss evidence; retrieved text can contain malicious instructions
Permissions and freshness must be enforced at retrieval time

followUps.question: RAG vs fine-tuning?
followUps.answer: RAG supplies external facts at inference time; fine-tuning changes model weights and is better suited to learned behavior or specialized formats. They can be combined.

followUps.question: Can RAG eliminate hallucinations?
followUps.answer: No. It reduces unsupported answers when retrieval and grounding work; measure faithfulness and refuse when evidence is inadequate.

followUps.question: When should you avoid RAG?
followUps.answer: For self-contained reasoning, stable facts already reliably handled by the model, or tiny structured datasets better served by direct SQL/API queries.

topics.title: Chunking strategies
topics.concept: Chunking divides source content into retrievable units. Fixed-size splitting is simple; recursive splitting respects paragraph/sentence boundaries; semantic splitting detects topic shifts; structure-aware splitting preserves headings, tables and code blocks. A chunk should represent a coherent answerable idea.
topics.example: A 40-page insurance PDF has eligibility, claims and exclusions sections. Splitting by headings keeps the “Exclusions” paragraph together instead of mixing it with unrelated claim instructions.
topics.interviewAnswer: I choose chunking based on document structure and query patterns. For policy PDFs I prefer heading-aware or recursive splitting, retain section titles and page metadata, and avoid splitting tables or clauses mid-thought. I compare chunking variants using retrieval Recall@k and downstream faithfulness rather than choosing one arbitrary chunk size.
steps: Extract layout, headings, tables and page references
Normalize OCR artifacts, remove repetitive headers and footers
Split on semantic/structural boundaries; add breadcrumb headers
Store chunk IDs, parent IDs and document versions
tradeoffs: Fixed-size is cheap but may break concepts
Semantic splitting costs more and can create uneven chunks
Tables and code often need custom parsing

followUps.question: What is semantic chunking?
followUps.answer: Embedding adjacent sentences and splitting where topic similarity drops; boundaries still require validation.

followUps.question: How do you chunk tables?
followUps.answer: Preserve table schema, headers and row relationships; consider table summaries for retrieval and original rows for answering.

followUps.question: What about PDFs with columns?
followUps.answer: Use layout-aware extraction first; naive text extraction can interleave columns and destroy meaning.

topics.title: Chunk size and overlap
topics.concept: Chunk size is a retrieval granularity choice, usually measured in model tokens. Small chunks can improve topical precision but lose context; large chunks preserve context but dilute embeddings and increase prompt tokens. Overlap duplicates boundary text to reduce information loss. There is no universally optimal size.
topics.example: A 1,200-token policy section split into ~400-token chunks with ~60-token overlap can preserve a clause that crosses a boundary. These are starting values, not best-practice constants.
topics.interviewAnswer: I start with a benchmark such as 300–600 tokens and 10–20% overlap for prose, then tune against representative questions. I watch Recall@k, answer accuracy, duplicate retrieval, index size and latency. For complex sections I retrieve small child chunks and expand to their parents instead of simply increasing every chunk size.
steps: Select a tokenizer aligned with your embedding/generation stack
Create a small labeled set of queries and relevant passages
Sweep chunk sizes and overlaps; compare retrieval and answer metrics
Inspect failure cases where boundaries separate necessary evidence
tradeoffs: More overlap increases storage, embedding cost and duplicate hits
Oversized chunks can exceed embedding model input limits
Chunk sizes should vary by document type

followUps.question: Why not 1,000 tokens everywhere?
followUps.answer: It may mix unrelated topics and lower precision; long legal clauses may need it, but short FAQ entries do not.

followUps.question: Does overlap always help?
followUps.answer: No. Excess overlap duplicates results and can crowd out distinct evidence.

followUps.question: What is a good starting point?
followUps.answer: For prose, try roughly 300–600 tokens with modest overlap, then validate on your dataset.

topics.title: Embedding models
topics.concept: An embedding model maps text into numeric vectors where semantically related inputs tend to have nearby representations. Dense embeddings support semantic search; sparse representations emphasize lexical signals. Query and document vectors must use a compatible model and preprocessing pipeline.
topics.example: “How can I reset my password?” and “I forgot my login credentials” can have similar embeddings even though they share few exact words.
topics.interviewAnswer: I select an embedding model using domain-specific retrieval benchmarks, language coverage, vector dimension, latency, privacy and cost. I embed documents offline and queries online using the same compatible model setup. When changing models, I version embeddings and rebuild or migrate the index instead of mixing incompatible vector spaces.
steps: Benchmark a few candidate models on labeled query–passage pairs
Check dimensionality, normalization, maximum input length and language support
Version model name, preprocessing and embedding configuration
Measure recall, throughput and storage per million vectors
tradeoffs: Larger vectors consume more RAM/storage
Domain-specific terminology and exact IDs may require BM25
Embedding similarity is not factual verification

followUps.question: Can I compare vectors from different embedding models?
followUps.answer: Not reliably; vector spaces differ unless explicitly aligned.

followUps.question: Why normalize vectors?
followUps.answer: For unit vectors, dot product equals cosine similarity; normalization also simplifies some ANN index choices.

followUps.question: What happens when the embedding model changes?
followUps.answer: Re-embed and reindex or maintain versioned parallel indexes during migration.

topics.title: Vector databases
topics.concept: A vector database stores embeddings and supports nearest-neighbor retrieval, often with approximate-nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexes such as HNSW. Production choices also depend on filtering, persistence, replication, tenant isolation, updates and observability. FAISS is primarily a similarity-search library; Qdrant, Milvus and Weaviate offer database-style services; PostgreSQL with pgvector is another option.
topics.example: A company stores 2 million policy chunks. The query embedding searches an ANN index for likely relevant passages, with a tenant filter preventing cross-customer access.
topics.interviewAnswer: I choose a vector store based on scale, operational complexity, filtering and latency rather than popularity. I store vector IDs and metadata with durable source references, use ANN for low-latency candidate retrieval, and benchmark recall against exact search. I also plan deletion, reindexing, backups and tenant-level authorization.
steps: Estimate vectors, dimensions, QPS and update frequency
Choose exact search or ANN; benchmark recall–latency tradeoff
Design metadata indexes and tenant filters
Implement upserts, deletion, versioning and monitoring
tradeoffs: ANN can miss true nearest neighbors
High-cardinality filters may affect performance
Vector stores do not replace relational systems for transactions

followUps.question: FAISS vs Qdrant?
followUps.answer: FAISS is a vector similarity library; Qdrant provides a service with filtering, persistence and APIs.

followUps.question: What is HNSW?
followUps.answer: A navigable multi-layer proximity graph for approximate nearest-neighbor search; tuning affects memory, speed and recall.

followUps.question: How do you delete a document?
followUps.answer: Delete/tombstone its chunk IDs, update source/version metadata, and verify that results no longer surface.

topics.title: Similarity search
topics.concept: Similarity search ranks candidate vectors by a distance or similarity function, often cosine, inner product or Euclidean distance. Exact kNN compares broadly; ANN sacrifices some recall for speed. top-k, score thresholds and diversity controls affect what reaches the LLM.
topics.example: A query about parental leave returns five semantically close policy paragraphs. Two may be near-duplicates, so MMR can favor a more diverse result set.
topics.interviewAnswer: I embed the query, apply authorization and metadata filters, retrieve top-k candidates using ANN, and inspect score distributions. I tune k and thresholds using labeled queries; when top results are redundant I consider maximal marginal relevance or reranking.
steps: Encode query with the retrieval model
Apply prefilters where supported
Run top-k similarity/ANN search
Deduplicate, diversify or rerank candidates
tradeoffs: High top-k increases recall but also cost/noise
Similarity scores are not calibrated probabilities
ANN index parameters affect recall and latency

followUps.question: What is MMR?
followUps.answer: Maximal Marginal Relevance balances relevance to the query against redundancy among selected documents.

followUps.question: Is top-5 always enough?
followUps.answer: No. Tune candidate count against recall and downstream context budget.

followUps.question: Can you threshold cosine at 0.8?
followUps.answer: Not universally; thresholds depend on model, corpus and score distribution.

topics.title: Cosine similarity
topics.concept: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two nonzero vectors: cos(a,b) = (a·b) / (||a|| ||b||). It ranges from −1 to 1 mathematically; actual embedding score distributions depend on the model. It compares orientation rather than magnitude.
topics.example: Vectors [1,0] and [2,0] have cosine 1 because they point in the same direction. [1,0] and [0,1] have cosine 0 because they are orthogonal.
topics.interviewAnswer: Cosine similarity compares embedding direction, so it is useful when vector magnitude should not determine relevance. I normalize embeddings when appropriate, then use cosine or equivalent dot product on unit vectors. I never interpret a cosine score as a confidence percentage; I calibrate thresholds with labeled examples.
steps: Compute dot product a·b
Compute each vector L2 norm
Divide dot product by product of norms
Rank vectors by score; handle zero vectors explicitly
tradeoffs: Cosine ignores magnitude
Equal similarity does not mean equal factual relevance
Dot product equals cosine only for unit-normalized vectors

followUps.question: Cosine vs Euclidean?
followUps.answer: Cosine compares direction; Euclidean measures geometric distance. For unit vectors their rankings are closely related.

followUps.question: What if one vector is zero?
followUps.answer: Cosine is undefined; reject or handle the zero vector explicitly.

followUps.question: Does cosine 0.9 mean 90% relevant?
followUps.answer: No. It is a geometric score, not a calibrated probability.

topics.code:
import numpy as np
a=np.array([1.,0.]); b=np.array([2.,0.])
cos = np.dot(a,b)/(np.linalg.norm(a)*np.linalg.norm(b))
print(cos)  # 1.0

topics.title: Metadata filtering
topics.concept: Metadata filtering restricts eligible documents by structured attributes such as tenant, ACL, date, language, product, region or version. It is different from semantic ranking: a filter enforces a hard constraint, while similarity scores rank within the eligible set.
topics.example: Question: “Show the 2026 India leave policy.” Filters tenant=acme, region=IN, year=2026 and user ACL before ranking relevant chunks.
topics.interviewAnswer: I treat metadata filters as a correctness and security boundary. I store stable tenant IDs, ACLs, timestamps and document versions. I apply authorization constraints in the retrieval layer—preferably before ANN search when supported—and verify no forbidden chunks appear even if the LLM is prompted to reveal them.
steps: Define consistent metadata schema and types
Translate explicit user constraints to structured filters
Enforce tenant and ACL filters server-side
Test filtered recall and permission boundaries
tradeoffs: Post-filtering can return fewer than k hits
Poor metadata quality leads to silent misses
Never rely on prompt instructions for access control

followUps.question: Pre-filter vs post-filter?
followUps.answer: Pre-filter limits the candidate pool before vector retrieval; post-filter removes matches afterward and can reduce recall/count.

followUps.question: Can the LLM enforce tenant isolation?
followUps.answer: No. Authorization belongs in the backend/search layer.

followUps.question: How do you filter by date?
followUps.answer: Store normalized timestamps or effective-date ranges, not just free-text dates.

topics.title: Hybrid search
topics.concept: Hybrid search combines lexical retrieval (often BM25) and semantic vector retrieval. Lexical matching captures exact terms, IDs and uncommon names; dense retrieval captures paraphrases. Fusion techniques such as Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) combine rankings without requiring raw scores to share a scale.
topics.example: Query “ERR_CONN_RESET in VPN guide” needs exact error-code matching, while “internet keeps disconnecting on work laptop” benefits from semantic matching. Hybrid search handles both.
topics.interviewAnswer: I use hybrid retrieval when the corpus mixes exact identifiers with natural-language questions. I retrieve candidates from BM25 and dense search in parallel, merge with RRF, deduplicate and optionally rerank the union. I validate the improvement against BM25-only and vector-only baselines, including latency.
steps: Index searchable text and embeddings
Run BM25 and dense retrieval concurrently
Fuse ranked lists using RRF or calibrated weighted scores
Rerank, filter and pass the final evidence set
tradeoffs: Two retrieval paths add operational cost
Raw BM25 and cosine scores should not be summed naively
Fusion weights and candidate counts need evaluation

followUps.question: Why RRF?
followUps.answer: It uses rank positions rather than incomparable raw BM25 and vector scores.

followUps.question: What is the RRF formula?
followUps.answer: Sum 1/(k + rank_i(d)) across retrieval lists where document d appears; k is a smoothing constant.

followUps.question: Does hybrid always win?
followUps.answer: No. For a narrow semantic corpus, extra lexical retrieval may add noise; measure performance.

topics.title: BM25
topics.concept: BM25 is a probabilistic lexical ranking function using term frequency, inverse document frequency and document-length normalization. It rewards matching informative query terms, with saturation so repeated terms do not increase score indefinitely. Typical tunable parameters include k1 and b.
topics.example: Search “invoice INV-92841” should prioritize the exact invoice identifier. A dense embedding may blur the digits, while BM25 rewards the matching token if the analyzer preserves it.
topics.interviewAnswer: BM25 is my lexical baseline for RAG because it is fast, interpretable and strong on exact keywords, error codes and product names. I pair it with dense retrieval when users also ask paraphrased questions, and I inspect tokenization and analyzers for IDs, acronyms and multilingual text.
steps: Tokenize/index documents with a suitable analyzer
Score term matches using IDF and saturated term frequency
Normalize for document length
Return ranked lexical candidates for fusion or direct retrieval
tradeoffs: Exact identifiers may require keyword fields rather than stemming
BM25 cannot infer synonyms without expansion
Analyzer design often matters more than minor parameter tuning

followUps.question: BM25 vs TF-IDF?
followUps.answer: BM25 adds term-frequency saturation and document-length normalization, generally making it a stronger retrieval baseline.

followUps.question: What do k1 and b control?
followUps.answer: k1 controls term-frequency saturation; b controls document-length normalization.

followUps.question: Why does BM25 fail on paraphrases?
followUps.answer: It primarily matches lexical tokens and may not recognize semantic equivalence.

topics.title: Reranking
topics.concept: Reranking reorders an initial shortlist with a more expensive relevance model. A cross-encoder jointly processes query and candidate passage, capturing interactions that separate bi-encoder embeddings cannot. It improves ordering but cannot recover documents absent from the candidate pool.
topics.example: Dense+BM25 retrieves 40 candidate chunks. A cross-encoder scores each against the question, and the top 6 are sent to the generator.
topics.interviewAnswer: I use a two-stage pipeline: inexpensive retrieval for broad recall, then a cross-encoder reranker for precision. I benchmark candidate pool size, top-n selection, relevance gains and p95 latency. If the correct document is not in the initial pool, I fix retrieval first rather than expecting reranking to solve it.
steps: Retrieve a broad candidate pool (for example 30–50)
Score query–passage pairs with a reranker
Sort and retain top-n with diversity or token-budget constraints
Measure nDCG/MRR and answer quality
tradeoffs: Cross-encoders are slower and costlier
Long candidates may be truncated
Reranking cannot fix missing retrieval candidates

followUps.question: Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder?
followUps.answer: Bi-encoder independently embeds query and documents for scalable search; cross-encoder jointly scores pairs for better fine-grained relevance.

followUps.question: How many documents should you rerank?
followUps.answer: Choose by latency budget and recall; 20–100 is a test range, not a rule.

followUps.question: Can an LLM rerank?
followUps.answer: Yes, but cost, latency, determinism and prompt-injection resistance must be evaluated.

topics.title: Query rewriting
topics.concept: Query rewriting transforms vague, conversational or noisy questions into a standalone retrieval query while preserving intent. It can resolve pronouns using chat history, expand acronyms or normalize spelling. Rewriting must not invent constraints or change the user’s meaning.
topics.example: Chat: “What is the leave policy?” followed by “What about contractors?” Rewrite the second query to “What is the leave policy for contractors?”
topics.interviewAnswer: For conversational RAG I separate the user’s original question from a retrieval-oriented rewritten query. The rewrite uses relevant chat context, preserves named entities and constraints, and is validated to avoid query drift. I log both queries so failures can be traced to rewriting versus retrieval.
steps: Collect the minimum relevant conversation history
Rewrite to a standalone, precise query
Preserve original names, dates, filters and negation
Retrieve using the rewritten query; answer the original intent
tradeoffs: LLM rewriting adds latency and cost
Bad rewrites can silently change intent
Sensitive history should not leak into unrelated searches

followUps.question: Rewrite vs summarize?
followUps.answer: Rewrite produces a retrieval query; summarization condenses broader context.

followUps.question: What is query drift?
followUps.answer: A rewrite changes the meaning or adds unsupported constraints, causing retrieval of the wrong evidence.

followUps.question: Should you always rewrite?
followUps.answer: No. Clear standalone queries may be better left unchanged.

topics.title: Multi-query retrieval
topics.concept: Multi-query retrieval generates multiple semantically distinct formulations of a question and retrieves for each. The union increases recall when a single wording misses relevant passages. Deduplication and fusion prevent redundant results from dominating.
topics.example: “How do I leave the company?” generates “employee resignation procedure”, “notice period rules”, and “exit clearance checklist”, retrieving different policy sections.
topics.interviewAnswer: I use multi-query when users ask broad or ambiguous questions. I generate a small set of intent-preserving variants, run retrieval in parallel, merge unique chunk IDs and rerank the combined set. I track recall improvement against extra tokens, queries and latency; for complex multi-part questions I may decompose rather than merely paraphrase.
steps: Generate 2–4 distinct query formulations
Run each through the same secured retriever
Union/deduplicate document IDs and fuse rankings
Rerank and cap evidence to the prompt budget
tradeoffs: More queries raise retrieval cost and noise
Variants can drift into unrelated topics
Multi-query paraphrasing differs from sub-question decomposition

followUps.question: Multi-query vs query rewriting?
followUps.answer: Rewriting usually yields one improved query; multi-query uses several variants for broader coverage.

followUps.question: How do you merge results?
followUps.answer: Deduplicate by stable chunk ID, then use RRF or reranking.

followUps.question: When is decomposition better?
followUps.answer: When a question requires distinct facts or steps, such as comparing policies across two regions.

topics.title: Parent-child retrieval
topics.concept: Parent-child retrieval embeds small child chunks for precise matching but returns larger parent sections for complete context. Each child stores a parent ID; a separate document store retrieves the parent after child search. The parent can be a section rather than the entire source document.
topics.example: A child chunk says “Employees may carry forward 10 days.” Its parent section contains eligibility and exceptions, preventing an incomplete answer.
topics.interviewAnswer: I index small child chunks to improve retrieval precision and retain larger parent sections in a document store. After finding relevant children, I fetch unique parents, enforce source permissions and pass only the relevant parent sections to the LLM. This balances search specificity with answer completeness.
steps: Create stable parent sections with source/version IDs
Split each parent into smaller child chunks and embed them
Search children; collect unique parent IDs
Fetch parents, deduplicate and trim to token budget
tradeoffs: Parents that are too large introduce noise
Multiple child hits can repeatedly fetch the same parent
Permission and version checks must apply to both layers

followUps.question: Why not embed parents directly?
followUps.answer: Large parents can dilute the specific signal that makes a passage retrievable.

followUps.question: Where are parents stored?
followUps.answer: A docstore, object store or relational database keyed by parent ID.

followUps.question: What if the parent exceeds the context window?
followUps.answer: Use section-level parents, extract relevant spans or apply contextual compression.

topics.title: Context compression
topics.concept: Context compression reduces retrieved evidence to query-relevant sentences, spans or summaries before generation. It saves tokens and removes distracting material, but aggressive compression may remove qualifiers, exceptions or citation anchors.
topics.example: A 2,000-token HR policy section contains only 180 tokens relevant to a question about maternity leave; an extractor keeps the relevant clause plus its exception.
topics.interviewAnswer: I apply contextual compression after retrieval when passages are long or noisy. I prefer extractive methods for high-stakes facts, preserve source offsets and citations, and compare answers before and after compression. I explicitly test whether exceptions and negations survive.
steps: Retrieve high-recall candidate documents
Select relevant spans or summarize with evidence preservation
Keep source IDs, page numbers and offsets
Check factual completeness and pass compressed evidence to LLM
tradeoffs: Abstractive compression may hallucinate
Compression can erase exceptions or units
Extra processing may outweigh token savings

followUps.question: Compression vs reranking?
followUps.answer: Reranking changes candidate order; compression changes the content/length of candidates.

followUps.question: Extractive vs abstractive?
followUps.answer: Extractive selects original spans; abstractive paraphrases and risks altering meaning.

followUps.question: How do you validate compression?
followUps.answer: Check that answer-bearing facts, negation and citations remain intact on a labeled set.

topics.title: Hybrid RAG
topics.concept: Hybrid RAG is an overloaded term. It commonly means RAG using hybrid lexical+dense retrieval, but can also describe systems combining structured SQL, knowledge graphs, APIs and vector search. Define the meaning explicitly in an interview. Hybrid search is a retrieval technique; hybrid RAG refers to the broader end-to-end architecture using it.
topics.example: A support assistant retrieves policy text using BM25+dense vectors, but queries PostgreSQL for a user’s live ticket status, then synthesizes a cited answer.
topics.interviewAnswer: When I say hybrid RAG, I clarify the architecture. In a search-centric system I mean BM25 plus dense retrieval, fused and reranked before generation. In a multi-source system I may also route structured questions to SQL or APIs. I choose each data source based on the type of truth needed, while preserving authorization and provenance.
steps: Classify query intent and needed source types
Route to lexical, vector, SQL, graph or API tools as appropriate
Merge or reconcile evidence with timestamps and provenance
Generate a source-grounded answer with conflict handling
tradeoffs: More sources increase orchestration complexity
Conflicting sources need explicit precedence rules
Live transactional facts belong in authoritative APIs/DBs

followUps.question: Hybrid RAG vs hybrid search?
followUps.answer: Hybrid search combines retrieval methods; hybrid RAG can describe the entire system that uses those methods and possibly other data sources.

followUps.question: When use SQL instead of vectors?
followUps.answer: For exact counts, aggregations, current balances and structured predicates.

followUps.question: How handle conflicting documents?
followUps.answer: Prefer authorized, effective, authoritative sources; surface uncertainty if conflict remains.

topics.title: Agentic RAG
topics.concept: Agentic RAG uses a controller or agent to decide whether, where and how to retrieve, possibly iterating through tools, decomposition and verification. Standard RAG often follows a fixed retrieve-then-generate flow. Agentic systems help with multi-hop questions but add cost, latency and failure modes.
topics.example: “Compare last quarter’s incidents with the current runbook and recommend actions.” An agent fetches incident metrics, searches runbooks, checks discrepancies and then drafts the answer.
topics.interviewAnswer: I use agentic RAG only when fixed retrieval is insufficient, such as multi-hop reasoning or tool selection across SQL, search and APIs. I constrain tools, budgets and iterations, enforce authorization at every call, and require evidence-based final answers. For simple FAQs I prefer deterministic RAG because it is cheaper and easier to test.
steps: Plan or classify the question and choose tools
Retrieve or call tools; inspect evidence sufficiency
Optionally reformulate, retrieve again or verify
Stop on budget/sufficiency limits and answer with citations
tradeoffs: Tool loops can explode latency and cost
Prompt injection can manipulate tool decisions
Agents need iteration limits, tracing and deterministic guardrails

followUps.question: Agentic vs standard RAG?
followUps.answer: Standard RAG follows a predetermined retrieval pipeline; agentic RAG dynamically chooses and repeats retrieval/tool steps.

followUps.question: How prevent infinite loops?
followUps.answer: Set max iterations, time/token budgets, stop conditions and fallback responses.

followUps.question: What is a multi-hop question?
followUps.answer: A question needing facts from multiple sources or sequential dependent retrieval steps.

topics.title: RAG hallucinations
topics.concept: RAG hallucinations are unsupported, invented or misattributed claims in generated answers. Causes include missing evidence, stale/contradictory chunks, irrelevant retrieval, lost qualifiers, poor prompts and model overgeneralization. A retrieved citation does not automatically make a claim true.
topics.example: A policy says “10 days carry-forward for permanent employees.” The assistant answers “All employees get 10 days,” ignoring the eligibility qualifier.
topics.interviewAnswer: I reduce RAG hallucinations by improving retrieval recall and precision, filtering stale sources, reranking, using explicit evidence-only prompts, and requiring abstention for unsupported claims. I evaluate claim-level faithfulness and citation support, not just fluent answer quality. I also test adversarial retrieved text as untrusted input.
steps: Classify errors: retrieval miss, evidence conflict, synthesis error
Improve retrieval and preserve qualifiers/versions
Require supported claims and an uncertainty fallback
Evaluate faithfulness, citation accuracy and abstention
tradeoffs: Prompting alone cannot guarantee groundedness
A highly relevant passage may still lack the answer
LLM-as-judge evaluations require calibration

followUps.question: What if retrieval returns nothing?
followUps.answer: Ask a clarification, say evidence is insufficient or escalate; do not fabricate an answer.

followUps.question: How distinguish retrieval from generation failure?
followUps.answer: Check whether the correct evidence was present in retrieved context before judging the generated response.

followUps.question: Can temperature 0 eliminate hallucinations?
followUps.answer: No. Lower temperature can reduce variability but does not ensure factual support.

topics.title: Citation/grounding
topics.concept: Grounding means every material factual claim is supported by retrieved authoritative evidence. Citations identify source documents and ideally exact page/section/span. A citation must actually entail the claim; attaching a plausible source URL is insufficient.
topics.example: Answer: “Contractors are excluded from carry-forward [HR Policy v4, §3.2].” A verifier checks that §3.2 really states that exclusion.
topics.interviewAnswer: I store source IDs, versions, page numbers and offsets during ingestion. At generation time I pass source-labeled evidence and require citations on factual claims. I validate that cited passages support those claims, reject inaccessible sources and handle unsupported answers with explicit uncertainty.
steps: Preserve provenance through extraction and chunking
Attach stable source IDs and page/section references
Generate claims with passage-level citations
Verify citation existence, authorization and entailment
tradeoffs: Citations can be fabricated by the model
Page numbers may shift across document versions
Multiple claims may need multiple supporting passages

followUps.question: Citation vs grounding?
followUps.answer: A citation is a reference; grounding is actual evidence support. Citations can be present without grounding.

followUps.question: How do you prevent fake citations?
followUps.answer: Restrict citations to retrieved IDs and validate IDs and supporting spans after generation.

followUps.question: How handle source updates?
followUps.answer: Version documents and ensure citation links resolve to the exact indexed version.

topics.title: RAG evaluation

def recall_at_k(retrieved, relevant, k):
    relevant = set(relevant)
    return len(set(retrieved[:k]) & relevant) / len(relevant) if relevant else 1.0

print(recall_at_k(["c", "a", "d"], {"a", "b"}, 3))  # 0.5
